Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones
A specific texture associated with the event

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I have to be on guard all the time
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: For a 55-year-old female bank teller with combat trauma, 'Bicycle' as a trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items imply interpersonal/loss and sensory trauma reminders, while bicycle is a highly specific cue with no support from threat, memory, or appraisal content and no clear combat linkage. This makes it clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'You can never know who will harm you' is too nonspecific relative to the rest of the profile. The threat items emphasize overt vigilance and reading faces/body language, and the appraisals also center betrayal and loss of meaning. This item implies diffuse interpersonal mistrust without a corresponding interpersonal memory or trigger pattern beyond betrayal, making the negative appraisal set less coherent with the otherwise combat/loss-focused formulation.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise organized around combat-linked threat, sensory triggers, and disjointed trauma memory, but the betrayal appraisal introduces a different interpersonal trauma theme that is not supported by the other selected items. With combat trauma, betrayal can occur, but here there are no corresponding triggers, memory content, or threat/appraisal items suggesting moral injury, friendly-fire, command betrayal, or interpersonal violation. This makes the betrayal item the main clinically incoherent element relative to the rest of the profile and formulation.

vignette:
Marisol is a 55-year-old divorced Latina woman who works as a bank teller in a mid-sized city in Texas. She came to the clinic after months of quiet deterioration, referred by her primary care physician who had grown concerned about her complaints of chronic fatigue and difficulty concentrating at work. What emerged across the first several sessions was a clinical picture rooted in events that had taken place more than two decades earlier, though they had lost none of their immediacy.

Marisol had served in the United States Army in the early 2000s and was deployed to Iraq as part of a support unit. One afternoon, during what had seemed like an unremarkable convoy movement, a roadside bomb detonated just ahead of the vehicle she was riding in. The blast was close enough that the percussion moved through her chest like a fist. In the chaos that followed, she found herself pressing her hands against the torn uniform of a fellow soldier, the coarse, blood-soaked fabric bunching under her fingers as she tried to keep pressure on a wound she could not see clearly through the smoke. That soldier did not survive. Marisol was evacuated, physically unharmed in any documented sense, and eventually returned stateside, where she left the military, married, raised two children, and built what looked from the outside like an ordinary life. The marriage ended eight years ago. The children are grown and live in other states.

For years she managed. Then, gradually, the management began to cost more than she had. She cannot now say with any precision when the shift happened, only that it did. When she tries to reconstruct the timeline of her symptoms, the thread slips away from her - she will begin to describe one period and find herself somewhere else entirely, the sequence scrambled, the chronology refusing to hold. She has told her therapist that the memory itself feels almost impossible to claim as her own: the extremity of it, the noise and the heat and what was under her hands, seems to belong to someone else's life, and yet her body responds as though it happened this morning.

At the bank, where she stands behind a counter for eight hours a day, the environment presents its challenges with regularity. A car backfiring in the parking lot, a door slamming hard across the lobby - any sharp, percussive sound can bring a wave of physical response that she has learned to hide behind a practiced stillness: her heart rate climbing, her hands going cold, her jaw tightening. She has become skilled at watching the faces of customers as they approach her window, reading their expressions and the set of their shoulders for information she cannot quite name but feels compelled to gather. She scans the lobby between transactions - the exits, the corners, the people standing in line - in a way that her colleagues have occasionally remarked upon, though she has deflected their comments. She has come to believe, in a way she finds difficult to articulate but impossible to dismiss, that the world does not offer safety as a baseline condition; it must be monitored for it, and even then it cannot be trusted.

A customer mentioning a bereavement - a parent lost, a spouse gone - can stop her mid-transaction. She has had to excuse herself to the back room on more than one occasion. The texture of certain rough fabrics, encountered unexpectedly, will sometimes produce a physical recoil that she cannot suppress and cannot explain to anyone around her.

Over the past year, Marisol has found herself increasingly unable to identify anything in her daily life that carries genuine weight or pleasure. Her work feels mechanical. Her apartment feels like a waiting room. She has described a sense that meaning has simply drained out of ordinary things, leaving their shapes intact but hollow.

What finally brought her to seek help was a conversation with her younger daughter over the phone, during which her daughter mentioned a neighbor's sudden death. Marisol ended the call abruptly and sat on her kitchen floor for an hour. She came to the clinic the following week. What she is most afraid of is that nothing she carries can be put back in order. What she is most hoping for, though she offered this quietly and without much apparent conviction, is that she might one day stop feeling like a threat is always about to arrive.
